# Tire Replacement Logic: Single vs. Pair on a Failed Set

A blown tire on a set that was recently installed is frustrating, but it forces you to make an immediate decision about your vehicle's safety and performance profile. In this specific scenario involving a 2012 Camry with Michelin Energy Saver A/S tires at 15,000 miles, the choice isn't just about cost; it's about managing tread depth variance and suspension dynamics.

The core technical constraint here is uniformity. Modern vehicles, especially those with anti-lock braking systems (ABS) and electronic stability control (ESC), rely on consistent tire diameters to function correctly. When you replace a single tire from a set of four that have already accumulated mileage, you introduce a mismatch in rolling circumference. The new tire will have significantly more tread depth than the remaining three 15,000-mile tires. This difference creates a variation in rotational speed between the wheels. While modern ABS systems are designed to handle some degree of slip ratio, extreme differences in diameter can trigger false warnings or, worse, reduce the system's ability to modulate brake pressure effectively during emergency stops.

From an implementation perspective, think of your vehicle like a distributed system where nodes must operate within specific tolerance thresholds. If one node (the new tire) has different latency characteristics (rolling resistance/diameter) than the others, the coordination logic (ESC/ABS) may struggle to optimize performance under load. While you might not notice immediate handling changes in normal driving conditions—as your personal experience with the single replacement suggests—the long-term risk lies in stress distribution across the suspension and drivetrain components.

The trade-off is financial versus mechanical integrity. Replacing a pair ensures that two wheels share similar wear characteristics, but it leaves the old tires mismatched against the new ones if you ever replace them again later. Some shops offer tire shaving to increase the diameter of worn tires to match a new one, effectively resetting the tread depth by removing material from the outer sidewall. However, this is not always feasible or recommended. As noted in your experience, Discount Tire does not offer this service. Attempting to shave tires yourself is ill-advised and can compromise structural integrity.

There is also the warranty angle to consider. Your Michelin Energy Saver A/S tires are warranted through 65,000 miles. A blowout at 15,000 miles due to a screw penetrating the center of the tread suggests a potential manufacturing defect or premature wear issue rather than normal degradation. In many cases, if you can prove the tire failed prematurely (often requiring a tread depth test and documentation), the manufacturer may cover the cost of replacing all four tires, not just one. This is a critical step before purchasing any replacement parts. If the warranty covers the set, installing only one tire defeats the purpose of the coverage and leaves you with three potentially compromised units if the failure mode was systemic to that batch.

In your specific case, the prorated cost from the original purchase ($35) versus the full retail price made the single replacement economically viable, even without shaving. The $25 restocking fee for cancelling the second order is a minor administrative cost compared to the expense of buying two additional tires immediately. However, proceed with caution: monitor your ABS/ESC warning lights and ensure you rotate the new tire after 500 miles to see if any drivetrain strain emerges that isn't present in the others.

If the warranty claim is denied or you decide to pay out of pocket for just one unit, accept that this is a temporary configuration. Plan to replace all four tires when the remaining three reach their service limit, ensuring you revert to a matched set before your next major service interval.
